title: What They Wanted Was So Small
deck: A room, real coffee, lipstick, and a glass paperweight show that life can exceed its political uses.
body: Edition note: Complete English translation of the Chinese essay. Full-book spoilers.
The note Julia slips to Winston contains just three words.
I love you.
She passes it to him in a corridor. She pretends to fall; he helps her up; the note finds its way into his hand. It takes him a long time to find a chance to open it.
Before this, he was certain the girl belonged to the Thought Police. He had even imagined killing her.
And what the note says is those three words.
What they do
Later, they rent a small room above a shabby junk shop.
What is in that room?
A bed. It takes up most of the room and has bugs.
A kerosene stove. They can cook on it.
A picture. An old church, hanging on the wall.
A glass paperweight. Winston bought it in the shop. It is something from the old days: a piece of glass with a tiny fragment of coral sealed inside.
No telescreen. This is the most important thing. The room has none of those screens that can watch as well as broadcast, so no one hears what they say inside it.
What do they do in that room?
They sleep. They make love. They brew coffee: real coffee, not the rationed substitute. Julia gets real sugar, real bread, and real jam on the black market.
She also gets hold of cosmetics. Once she makes up her face, still wearing her overalls, and says she will get a real dress later. Winston thinks she looks like a woman.
They lie there talking. They watch the woman outside the window singing as she does the washing.
That is all.
None of these things is useful
Now look carefully at that list.
The meaning of these things goes beyond resistance.

They do seek out O'Brien and try to join the Brotherhood. That is a political action that leads them into a trap. But the days they spend in this room cannot be measured solely by their usefulness to resistance.
What they do is eat real food, drink real coffee, put on lipstick, make love, talk, and look out of the window.
The value of these things does not depend on whether they can overthrow the regime.
And this is the first thing this essay wants to say: it is precisely because these things are of no use that they belong to them.
The first essay described the machinery's aim: closing every gap, in language, in feeling, in fact.
And the gaps are closed according to use.
What does the Party seek to manage? Production, loyalty, hatred, war, history, everything that might develop into opposition. These are all useful things, so they have all been taken over.
But the taste of a cup of real coffee, the feel of lipstick on the lips, an afternoon spent lying down and looking out of the window: the meaning of these things is not on that list of uses.
The Party has not forgotten to forbid them. It deliberately suppresses sexual pleasure, but that cannot turn these experiences into things with only political uses.
How Julia sees it
Julia is completely different from Winston, and the contrast is one of the best things in the novel.

Winston is a man of theories. He cares about truth, about whether history has been altered, about what two plus two equals. He reads the forbidden book avidly. He wants to understand how all this works.
Julia has no interest in any of it.

He tells her about the falsification of history, and she falls asleep as she listens. He explains the Party's theories, and she says they have nothing to do with her. She is not even especially concerned with whether the Party's claims are true or false. Her attitude is: let them say what they like; I will get on with what I want to do.
She is twenty-six, works in the Fiction Department, and is an active member of the Junior Anti-Sex League. She ties that scarlet sash tightly, because that is the best way to avoid suspicion.
Her principle is: be faultless on the surface; in private, do as you please.
She has had affairs with many people. She steals. She is a practiced liar. She says she has been doing this since she was sixteen.

At first, Winston rather looks down on this attitude. He thinks she is merely a “rebel from the waist down”: she resists only the rules that press directly upon her, and cares nothing about the larger issues.
But what happens later in the novel shows that her way comes closer to the point than his.
One thing she understands before he does
One conversation is crucial.
Winston tells her that sooner or later they will be caught, forced to confess, and remade.
Julia says: they can make you say anything, but they cannot make you believe it. They cannot get inside you.

Winston thinks she is right. Later he thinks the same thing himself: your bones can be broken; you can be forced to betray people, forced to say anything at all. But as long as that one thing inside you remains, you have not lost.
This is the most important conviction in the first half of the book. The third essay will return to how it proves wrong.
But here we must first see the half of her statement that is right.

Her attention is on the days they can still live now, rather than on a distant political victory. When Winston earlier says “we are the dead,” she objects: we are not dead yet. Only in the conversation just before their arrest does she, too, say “we are the dead.”
She is speaking about the present: at this moment, they have not reached this place inside me.

And the way she lives puts that statement into practice: although she, too, has gone with Winston to seek out O'Brien, she gives more thought to the lipstick, real coffee, and afternoon at hand. These are not things the Party has forgotten to control. They are the life she still wants to live, at the risk of arrest.
She lives in the gaps.
The glass paperweight
One object recurs throughout the novel and deserves a look of its own.
The glass paperweight.
Winston buys it at the junk shop. The proprietor says it is more than a hundred years old. A tiny piece of coral is enclosed inside. It is heavy, beautiful, and pleasant to the touch.
And it is utterly useless.

It can do nothing. You cannot eat it, wear it, or exchange it for money: people in that age do not buy such things. There is not even a category of “antique” for it to belong to, because the past has been deleted and no one knows what period it comes from.
Winston explains why he wants it himself: he says that what attracts him is precisely its uselessness.
Later he has another thought: the paperweight is like a little world, with himself and Julia inside, sealed in the glass, time stopped around them.
This is one of the most beautiful passages in the novel. It is also one of its cruelest pieces of foreshadowing.
Because when the Thought Police eventually burst into the room, someone smashes the paperweight on the floor.
The book describes it breaking. The little piece of coral rolls out, pitifully small.
There was a telescreen in the room all along
Now we come to the most painful part of this essay.
That picture: the old church hanging on the wall.
The telescreen is behind it.
From the first time they enter the room, the screen is there on the wall, behind that picture, watching and listening all the while.
Every word they say is recorded.
Their whispered conversations in bed, Julia's “they cannot get inside you,” their promises to one another, the history Winston recounts: all of it is overheard.
And Charrington, the owner of the junk shop, belongs to the Thought Police.
The kindly old man, the man who sold Winston the paperweight, who talked with him about old nursery rhymes, who rented them the upstairs room: he is the one who laid the trap.
On the day of their arrest, Charrington's appearance changes. He stands upright. His expression is different; so is his voice. Only then does Winston realize he is not actually old.
This is one of the coldest reversals in the book.
Because it means that from beginning to end, the room was a place prepared for them.
They did not find a gap. Someone prepared a gap for them and waited for them to walk into it.
Was what they kept unreal, then?
We must stop here and ask a question. Otherwise everything said so far has been for nothing.
If the room was a trap from the start, do the days they lived inside it still count?
This is the question the essay really has to answer.
We have to distinguish two things.
The room was a lie. It was a trap, an observation post, a place for gathering evidence. There is no room for doubt about that.
But the coffee was real. Julia wearing lipstick was real. Those afternoons when they lay talking were real. The song of the woman doing the washing outside the window was real.
Both things are true at once.
Behind the telescreen, the Thought Police watch them make love, drink coffee, and talk nonsense. And what those moments give them does not vanish because someone sees it.

Because none of it is for the telescreen. It needs no audience, no recognition. It does not have to remain secret in order to be real. A cup of real coffee tastes the same when someone watches you drink it.
The Party can raid the room and take them away. It cannot make those months not have happened.
And that is precisely what this regime cares about. It cares about this very much.
As the first essay explained, it wants to delete from “existence” whatever should not be there. To vaporize a person is to say that he has never existed.
But what has already happened is the one thing this machinery cannot deal with.
It can destroy records, alter newspapers, make everyone say that an event never happened.
It cannot make the event not have happened.
What they wanted was so small
Finally, we come to where this essay lands.
Look back over the list of things Winston and Julia do as they live in that room:

Eating real jam. Drinking real coffee. Wearing lipstick. Making love. Renting a room without a telescreen. Buying a glass paperweight. Lying together and talking. Watching the woman outside the window sing.
Even these things alone are forbidden.

And this system, with the force of an entire state behind it, the Ministry of Truth, the Ministry of Love, the Thought Police, telescreens, informers, children who report their parents: it hunts them not only because they try to take part in resistance, but also because it will not let those days of private life belong to them.
This deserves a pause.
If what a person wants is power, the regime can negotiate. If wealth, it can provide it. If status, it can arrange it. All of these appear in its accounts.
The taste of a cup of coffee does not.
So it cannot deal with this by giving. It can only deal with it by arresting.
It has to arrest people because it has no way to bring that thing into its service.
What Winston and Julia want in those days is so small, so small it hardly seems worth mentioning. And the machinery of this state will not leave even these small things alone.
Next
After his arrest, Winston is taken to the Ministry of Love.
Waiting for him there is O'Brien.

Winston has always thought O'Brien was a comrade. He believed the man belonged to the underground organization. He had visited O'Brien's home, drunk wine, sworn an oath, and later received the forbidden book through a briefcase exchange.
That, too, was a trap.
O'Brien is a member of the Inner Party, one of the people who operate this machinery. And the time and patience he spends on Winston are out of all proportion.
He has not come to punish him.
The next essay is about O'Brien, and about the monologue in this book that sounds least like a villain speaking.
Because O'Brien will tell Winston what the Party actually wants. And what he says is unlike everything we imagine about tyranny.
George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four, published in 1949. Names and terms in the Chinese essay follow Dong Leshan's translation.

review.full_reread: Read all four Chinese bodies and all four complete en translations, titles, decks and index. Reread every changed unit against the final approved wording and its surrounding argument. Earlier review evidence is retained in review_history, not current pending status.
review.structure: All paragraph, heading and inline-emphasis boundaries preserved; all unamended prose units unchanged.
review.interpretive_boundaries: Original authorial judgments retained. Source observations outside the approved change set remain historical context; this pass makes no new claim of exhaustive independent novel or publication-history verification.
semantic_checks: Photograph: conscious recognition and concealment, then destruction after about ten minutes through fear; no reflex or pre-awareness claim remains.
Private life: the Brotherhood attempt remains explicit, while value exceeds usefulness to resistance; deliberate suppression of sexual pleasure is not confused with a forgotten prohibition.
Dress is a future intention while Julia remains in overalls; lipstick replaces the invented worn dress in both sensory examples.
Julia rejects the earlier dead claim and repeats it only just before arrest; present life is distinguished from distant political victory.
Cross-references now point to essay three; forbidden book arrives later through a briefcase exchange.
Pain is controlled by a dial, without asserting an electrical mechanism; the two final sentences are the ending of the main narrative.
Publication: American Book-of-the-Month Club deletion request and refusal; the importance of final placement is explicitly the essay’s reading.

Proles: less intensive ideological training coexists with surveillance and removal of threats; no blanket illiteracy claim; the courtyard is reached by power without exhausting the meaning of the song.

Preserved the complete room/trap/real-experience argument, authorial claim that past events cannot be undone, stronger judgment about totality, and cautious appendix reading without supplying a new proof or ending.

review_history.stage: Complete-translation review before approved source corrections

review.coverage: All 114 source units translated in order, with all nine headings, scenes, reversals, the room-versus-experience distinction, and the transition to O'Brien.
prior_edition_findings: The previous approximately 507-word essay omitted the love note, Julia's detailed position, the inner-heart conviction, Charrington's change at the arrest, the full argument that events cannot be made not to have happened, and the next-essay transition.
It added a discussion of aesthetic attention and the political movement the room might justify. That substitute argument has been removed.

source_questions.issue: Julia's dress is treated as something worn. Part II, Chapter 4 describes makeup and a plan to obtain a dress, while she still wears overalls. Original claim retained pending author decision.

Statements that the lovers never contacted others or made plans, and the exhaustive crimes list, omit their attempt to join the Brotherhood in Part II, Chapter 8. A narrower distinction between ordinary life and effective organized opposition would preserve the essay's argument. Retained pending decision.

Part II, Chapter 3 has Julia resisting Winston's fatalism; she repeats his words about being dead only in Chapter 10. The broad account of her having no future expectation conflates these moments. Retained pending decision.

The claim that the Party did not think to prohibit these pleasures conflicts with its express hostility to sexual pleasure in Part I, Chapter 6 and Julia's explanation in Part II, Chapter 3. Experiential value exceeding the Party's purposes is a distinct argument and should not be confused with absence of prohibition. Retained pending decision.

The initial absence of a telescreen is the lovers' mistaken belief. Continuous listening is established; continuous viewing specifically through the covered telescreen is less secure, because Part II, Chapter 10 marks visibility after the picture falls. Wider photographic surveillance is confirmed in Part III, Chapter 4. Retained without inventing a mechanism.
Absolute inability to buy or exchange the paperweight is rhetorical and sits against Winston's purchase of it. Retained as authorial rhetoric, not independently strengthened.
The forbidden book is delivered later, not handed over during the visit to O'Brien's home. The original sentence may compress separate events; retained pending clarification.
The forward reference names essay four, while Room 101 is treated in essay three and summarized in essay four. Retained pending editorial decision.

review.style: Preserved short sentences, lists, repeated small pleasures, and the delayed trap reveal. Source uncertainties are recorded rather than silently repaired.
review.full_reread: All source and translated units were reread together as the four-essay batch; structure, emphasis, voice, transitions, and unresolved source claims were checked.
